title: Endocrine System and Diabetes
tagline: The pituitary, thyroid and adrenals, diabetes, bone and calcium, and reproductive hormones
summary: Hormones coordinate growth, metabolism and reproduction. This course covers the hypothalamus and pituitary, thyroid and adrenal disease, diabetes mellitus and its complications, bone and calcium metabolism, reproductive endocrinology and endocrine emergencies.
overview: Hormones are the body's slower signalling system. They travel in the blood, act on receptors in distant tissues, and are organised into axes closed by negative feedback. That organisation makes endocrine disease unusually logical to diagnose: almost every hormone result is read as a pair, the gland's product beside the signal that drives it, and the pattern points to the gland, the pituitary or the hypothalamus.

The course follows the axes in order: the hypothalamus and pituitary, including tumours and the control of water; the thyroid; the adrenal cortex and medulla; diabetes mellitus in two chapters, one on mechanisms and treatment and one on hypoglycaemia, ketoacidosis and long-term complications; calcium and bone; and reproductive endocrinology from puberty to the menopause. A final chapter gathers the emergencies, from adrenal crisis and thyroid storm to the hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state and severe hyponatraemia.

Numbers matter throughout: calculated osmolality, adjusted calcium, the anion gap, HbA1c units, the time to reach a drug's steady state, insulin dose arithmetic and the predictive value of screening tests. Clinical statements follow current UK guidance (NICE, the Joint British Diabetes Societies, the Society for Endocrinology) with international guidance where it is standard. Doses are illustrative principles; real prescribing follows current guidelines and an individual plan.
outcomes: Explain hypothalamic–pituitary control of each endocrine axis and use paired hormone results and dynamic tests to localise a lesion to gland, pituitary or hypothalamus.
Recognise and outline the investigation and management of pituitary tumours, hypopituitarism, hyperprolactinaemia, acromegaly, arginine vasopressin deficiency and resistance, and SIADH.

Describe thyroid hormone synthesis, transport and action; interpret thyroid function tests; and outline the management of hypothyroidism, thyrotoxicosis, thyroid disease in pregnancy, and thyroid nodules and cancer.

Explain adrenal physiology and the presentation, diagnosis and management of adrenal insufficiency (including glucocorticoid-induced suppression), Cushing's syndrome, primary aldosteronism, phaeochromocytoma and the adrenal incidentaloma.

Distinguish the types of diabetes by mechanism, apply the diagnostic criteria, interpret HbA1c and glucose-monitoring data, and explain the principles of drug and insulin treatment and sick-day rules.
Recognise and outline the management of hypoglycaemia and diabetic ketoacidosis, and explain the mechanisms, screening and prevention of microvascular and macrovascular complications.
Describe calcium, phosphate and vitamin D physiology; investigate abnormal calcium; and outline the assessment and treatment of osteoporosis, osteomalacia and Paget's disease.

Explain the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal axis and the menstrual cycle, and outline the assessment of disordered puberty, amenorrhoea, PCOS, premature ovarian insufficiency, the menopause and male hypogonadism.

Outline the resuscitation-first management of endocrine emergencies, including the hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state, adrenal crisis, thyroid storm, myxoedema coma, severe hyponatraemia, calcium emergencies and pituitary apoplexy.

history.title: The liver as an organ of sugar
history.detail: Claude Bernard discovers glycogen and the liver's production of glucose, and shows that a puncture in the floor of the fourth ventricle causes glycosuria, evidence that blood sugar is regulated as part of a stable internal environment.

history.title: Pancreatectomy and sugar
history.detail: Oskar Minkowski and Joseph von Mering remove a dog's pancreas in Strasbourg and produce fatal diabetes, showing that the pancreas prevents diabetes and starting the search that ended with insulin.

history.title: Chemical messengers
history.detail: William Bayliss and Ernest Starling show that acid in the duodenum releases a blood-borne substance, secretin, that makes the pancreas secrete; in 1905 Starling introduces the word hormone for such chemical messengers.

history.title: Thyroid surgery made safe
history.detail: Theodor Kocher of Bern receives the Nobel Prize for his work on the physiology, pathology and surgery of the thyroid gland. His careful technique made thyroidectomy safe, and his observation of hypothyroidism after total removal helped show what the gland does.

history.title: Isolation of insulin
history.detail: At the University of Toronto, Frederick Banting and Charles Best, in John Macleod's laboratory, prepare pancreatic extracts that lower blood glucose in diabetic dogs, and James Collip purifies them. In January 1922, 14-year-old Leonard Thompson becomes the first person treated successfully with insulin.

history.title: Cushing's syndrome
history.detail: Harvey Cushing, the American neurosurgeon who pioneered pituitary surgery, describes a group of patients with obesity of the trunk, hypertension, purple striae and weakness, and links the syndrome to small basophil adenomas of the pituitary.

history.title: Cortisone
history.detail: Philip Hench, Edward Kendall and Tadeus Reichstein share the Nobel Prize for work on the hormones of the adrenal cortex. Kendall and Reichstein isolated the corticosteroids, and in 1948 Hench gave cortisone to a woman with rheumatoid arthritis with dramatic effect, beginning the era of glucocorticoid therapy and its adverse effects.

history.title: Measuring the unmeasurable
history.detail: Rosalyn Yalow and Solomon Berson describe radioimmunoassay, using antibodies and radioactively labelled insulin to measure hormones at tiny concentrations in blood. Almost all later hormone assays build on the method, and Yalow receives the Nobel Prize in 1977.

history.title: Human insulin made in bacteria
history.detail: Scientists at Genentech, with collaborators at the City of Hope, produce human insulin in bacteria using recombinant DNA. Biosynthetic human insulin is approved in 1982, the first medicine made by genetic engineering.
